content: This test should also be conducted with the sprayer placed horizontally, with the strap side facing downward. Tank Capacity: The size of the tank for manually carried equipment depends on the maximum weight an operator can carry. For mechanized equipment, the tank size should correspond to the operational duration of the engine under normal conditions. The spray tank must be designed to allow complete drainage, either through valves and hoses leading to the nozzle or directly from the nozzle body when the control flow valve is closed. Tank Markings: Tanks must have permanent graduations marked at 1-liter intervals for tanks up to 10 liters and at 5-liter intervals for larger tanks. The maximum liquid level should also be indicated. For metal tanks, where the liquid level is not visible, manufacturers should provide a device or level gauge to help operators determine the correct liquid level during filling. Pesticide Tank Opening and Filter: The tank opening must be at least 90 mm wide to facilitate rapid filling without spillage. A filter should be installed at the filler opening to prevent splashing and to hold sealed water-soluble pesticide bags or sachets. Using sealed water-soluble bags eliminates direct contact between the operator and the concentrated pesticide, creating a closed transfer system. For fogging equipment with smaller openings, a filter funnel or closed transfer system should be used. The tank lid must remain attached during filling, and for compression sprayers, the filler opening should be separate from the pump mechanism to avoid removing the pump during refilling. Sprayer Tank Drainage: After use, the tank should be thoroughly washed and cleaned before storage or further use. The tank must be designed to allow complete drainage to prevent liquid from being stored inside. Straps for Manually Carried Equipment: Manually carried equipment should have one or two shoulder straps, and lever-operated sprayers should also include a waist strap to minimize tank movement during operation. Straps must be wide enough to prevent discomfort, with a minimum width of 50 mm. Adjustable straps are required, and for knapsack sprayers, the width should be 50 ± 5 mm. Hose Requirements: It should not kink or flatten, ensuring free flow. Hose connections must be user-replaceable, allowing for cutting and refitting if damaged, provided the length remains acceptable. Droplet Spectrum: The droplet size requirements depend on the type of spray application. For space treatments, droplets smaller than 30 µm in diameter are ideal to remain airborne longer, with an optimal range of 10–15 µm for most vector species. For residual wall spraying, less than 5% of the spray volume should consist of droplets smaller than 30 µm to minimize inhalation risks. When applying larvicides to water surfaces, droplet sizes should exceed 200 µm for rapid fallout unless vegetation is present, in which case granules are recommended. Noise Levels: If the noise level near the operator’s ear exceeds 85 decibels, ear protection must be provided and used. This requirement should be permanently marked on the equipment and included in the operating manual. Markings: The equipment must have clear markings indicating the manufacturer’s name, contact details, machine type, date of manufacture or serial number, and the position of key components. On/off positions for valves or switches, nozzle sizes, and flow restrictors must also be clearly visible. User Manual: Pesticide application equipment must include a clear, illustrated user manual detailing operation methods, calibration, safety precautions, maintenance procedures, and essential spare parts. Field Use: Operators should maintain a record of equipment use on a Spray History card, including maintenance dates and spare parts used. New equipment types and brands require field evaluation following initial laboratory testing. Compression Sprayer Description: Compression sprayers are primarily used for residual wall spraying and larvicide application. Knapsack Sprayers: Knapsack sprayers, often lever-operated, are used for larvicide application but are unsuitable for indoor residual spraying. They consist of a tank with two shoulder straps and a waist strap, a manually operated pump, a hose connecting the pump to the lance, and a lance with a trigger valve, control flow valve, and nozzle. The pump lever should be at least 400 mm long and operate within 20–30 strokes per minute to deliver over 70 liters per hour. Motorized Knapsack Mist Blowers: These are used for rapid treatment of open water bodies and barrier treatments around houses. They feature an engine-driven fan producing a high-velocity airstream to project pesticide liquid at least 10 meters upwards. The engine should be lightweight (<12 kg) and equipped with vibration-dampening mounts, easy-start mechanisms, and padded backrests for operator comfort. The fuel tank should support at least one hour of operation without refueling. Portable Cold Foggers: Cold foggers are hand-carried or knapsack-mounted aerosol generators used for space treatments in buildings and outdoor areas inaccessible to vehicles. They produce fine droplets for effective pesticide application.
